definition: A security method that requires users to provide two different types of identification before accessing an account, typically combining something you know with something you have.
metaDescription: Learn about two factor authentication (2FA) - a security method using two verification steps to protect your accounts from unauthorized access.
simpleExplanation: Two factor authentication adds an extra layer of security to your accounts. Instead of just entering a password, you also need to provide a second form of proof that it's really you, like a code sent to your phone or generated by an app.
whyItMatters: Even if someone steals or guesses your password, they still can't access your account without the second factor. This dramatically reduces the risk of account takeovers, identity theft, and data breaches affecting your personal information.
technicalDetail: 2FA typically combines authentication factors from different categories: knowledge factors (passwords, PINs), possession factors (phones, hardware tokens), and inherence factors (biometrics). The most common implementation uses SMS codes, authenticator apps generating time-based one-time passwords (TOTP), or hardware security keys.

examples.explanation: After entering your username and password, the bank sends a 6-digit code to your registered phone number that you must enter to complete the login process.
When logging into Gmail from a new device, you enter your password and then use an authenticator app like Google Authenticator to generate a time-sensitive code for verification.
Facebook can be configured to require both your password and a code from your phone via SMS or authenticator app whenever you log in from an unrecognized device.
